name: Authentication
explanation: Verifying who a user is, for example with a password, a one-time code or a sign-in provider such as Google.
synonyms: login;sign in;jwt
triggers: log in;sign up;password;who the user is;user account;register
requirements: Allow long passwords, at least 64 characters, and reject known breached passwords;Give the same error for a wrong username or a wrong password;Limit repeated failed logins per account and per IP address;Send login forms and session cookies only over HTTPS;Offer two-factor authentication;Require at least 8 characters, or 15 when the password is the only factor;Allow password managers and pasting, and never make a memory test or puzzle the only way to sign in;Never require character mixes or regular password changes, and accept spaces and Unicode
done_when: Login errors never reveal whether an account exists;Repeated wrong passwords are slowed down or blocked

name: Authorization and roles
explanation: Deciding what a signed-in user is allowed to do, usually through roles or permissions.
synonyms: access control;rbac;permissions;user roles
triggers: admin only;only admins;allowed to;who can see;restrict access;not allowed;who can;can approve;only managers;manager role
requirements: Check permissions on the server for every request, not only by hiding buttons;Deny by default, and give each role only what it needs;Check that the user may access the specific record, not only that they are signed in;Keep permission checks in one shared place instead of copied around;Add automated tests that check each role is refused what it may not do
done_when: Changing an id in the URL never shows another user's data;A user without permission gets 403 even when calling the API directly

name: Password hashing
explanation: Storing passwords as slow, salted hashes (such as bcrypt or Argon2) so they cannot be read if the database leaks.
synonyms: bcrypt;argon2;salted hash
triggers: store passwords;save passwords;password safely;secure passwords;encrypt password;stored safely;passwords stored;storing passwords
requirements: Hash passwords with Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt, never plain SHA or MD5;Let the library create a unique salt for every password;Tune the work factor so one hash takes a noticeable fraction of a second;Never log, email or store passwords in plain text;Rehash with stronger settings when users next sign in
done_when: The database contains no readable or reversible passwords;Two users with the same password have different hashes

name: Input sanitization and escaping
explanation: Treating user input as untrusted and escaping or validating it to prevent attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS).
synonyms: sql injection;xss;escaping;parameterized queries
triggers: hack;malicious input;safe from attacks;user input;security;script tag;html in input;inject;typed code
requirements: Validate input on the server against allowed types, lengths and formats;Use parameterized queries or an ORM, never SQL built from strings;Escape output for where it goes: HTML, attributes, URLs or JavaScript;Avoid innerHTML with user content, or sanitize it with a library such as DOMPurify;Add a Content Security Policy as a second line of defence;Check business rules on the server, such as prices, quantities and step order, never trusting the client;Redirect only to allowed URLs or relative paths, never to any URL taken from the request;Never rely on globals or document properties that user HTML with id or name attributes could override
done_when: Script tags or SQL quotes typed by a user are shown as plain text or rejected;Security scanners find no injection or XSS problems

name: Single sign-on (SSO)
explanation: Letting users sign in with an existing account from a provider such as Google, Microsoft or their company, usually through OAuth or OpenID Connect.
synonyms: sso;oauth;openid connect;social login;saml;single sign-on
triggers: sign in with google;login with google;google account;microsoft account;github login;company account
requirements: Use a proven OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect library instead of writing the flow yourself;Use the authorization code flow with PKCE, and check the state parameter;Verify the ID token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry;Link accounts by the provider's user id, not by email alone;Handle the user cancelling and the provider being unavailable;Send and check a nonce in OpenID Connect sign-ins to stop token replay;For SAML, validate signed assertions with a maintained library, and check audience, recipient, expiry and replay
done_when: Signing in with the provider finds or creates the right account;A forged or expired token is rejected

name: Two-factor authentication (2FA)
explanation: Asking for a second proof of identity after the password, such as a code from an authenticator app, a text message or a security key.
synonyms: 2fa;mfa;multi-factor authentication;one-time password;otp;totp
triggers: two factor;code from their phone;verification code;second step;authenticator app;extra security;login code;security key
requirements: Support an authenticator app (TOTP) or passkeys, and treat SMS codes as weaker;Give recovery codes when two-factor is turned on;Rate-limit code attempts;Ask for the password or a code before turning two-factor off;Let users trust a device for a limited time only;Offer a phishing-resistant option, such as passkeys or security keys;Never use email as the second factor
done_when: Signing in on a new device always asks for the second factor;A lost phone can be handled with a recovery code

name: Session management
explanation: Keeping a user signed in between requests with a session or token, and deciding when that ends, for example after inactivity or with a remember-me option.
synonyms: session;session timeout;refresh token;idle timeout
triggers: logged out;getting logged out;log the user out;stay logged in;remember me;keep me signed in;after inactivity;doing nothing;session expires
requirements: Keep the session in a cookie with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite set;Create a new session id after login;End sessions after inactivity and after a maximum lifetime;Make logout end the session on the server too;Let users see and end their other sessions;Warn users before a session times out, and let them extend it;Detect signs of a stolen session, such as a sudden IP or device change, and ask the user to sign in again;For sensitive apps, end sessions after about 1 hour idle and 24 hours in total
done_when: After logout, the old session cookie no longer works;Scripts on the page cannot read the session cookie

name: Password reset
explanation: Letting a user who forgot their password choose a new one through a time-limited link sent to their email.
synonyms: forgot password;reset link;password recovery
triggers: forgot my password;forgot their password;reset password;change password
requirements: Show the same message whether or not the email has an account;Send a random, single-use link that expires within about an hour;Store only a hash of the reset token;End other sessions after the password changes;Rate-limit reset requests;Build the reset link from a configured base URL, never from the request Host header;Never use security questions or password hints, for sign-in or for account recovery
done_when: Using a reset link twice, or after it expires, fails;The reset form never reveals which emails are registered

name: Email verification
explanation: Confirming that a new user owns their email address by sending a link or code they must click or enter.
synonyms: verify email;email confirmation;confirm email
triggers: confirm their email;verification link;email is real;activate account;confirm the account
requirements: Send a random, single-use link or code that expires;Explain what to do if the email does not arrive, with a rate-limited resend button;Verify again when the user changes their email address;Limit what unverified accounts can do
done_when: The link verifies the account once, and old links stop working;Resending is possible but limited

name: CSRF protection
explanation: Stopping other websites from submitting forms or requests on behalf of a signed-in user, using anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies.
synonyms: csrf;xsrf;cross-site request forgery;csrf token;samesite cookie
triggers: from another site;forged request;submit forms from;on behalf of the user
requirements: Use the framework's CSRF tokens for every form and state-changing request;Set SameSite=Lax or Strict on session cookies;Never change data in response to GET requests;Check the Origin header on state-changing requests
done_when: A form posted from another website is rejected;Every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE without a valid CSRF token is rejected

name: HTTPS and TLS
explanation: Encrypting traffic between the browser and the server with a TLS certificate, so the address starts with https and shows a padlock.
synonyms: https;ssl;tls;ssl certificate;lets encrypt
triggers: not secure warning;padlock;secure connection;certificate
requirements: Serve every page over HTTPS, and redirect HTTP to HTTPS;Turn on HSTS so browsers always use HTTPS;Renew certificates automatically, for example with Let's Encrypt;Allow only TLS 1.2 and newer;Load all scripts, images and styles over HTTPS too;Allow only strong cipher suites with forward secrecy, such as the Mozilla intermediate configuration
done_when: The browser shows a secure connection with no mixed-content warnings;An SSL test such as SSL Labs gives at least an A grade

name: Cookie consent
explanation: A banner that asks visitors for permission before setting non-essential cookies, as required by laws such as the GDPR.
synonyms: cookie banner;gdpr;consent banner;privacy banner
triggers: accept cookies;cookie popup;privacy law;ask permission;tracking consent
requirements: Set no analytics or marketing cookies before the user agrees;Make rejecting as easy as accepting, on the same screen;Let users change their choice later from a link on every page;Remember the choice and record when consent was given;Explain what each cookie category is for
done_when: Rejecting cookies means no tracking cookies are set;The banner works with the keyboard and with a screen reader

name: Passkeys (WebAuthn)
explanation: Signing in with the device's fingerprint, face or PIN instead of a password, using the WebAuthn standard.
synonyms: passkey;webauthn;fido2;biometric login;passwordless login;fingerprint;face id
triggers: sign in with fingerprint;login with face id;login without a password;touch id;no password login;windows hello;instead of a password
requirements: Use a maintained WebAuthn library on the server to check registrations and sign-ins;Check the challenge, origin and relying party id on every response;Create a new random challenge for each attempt, and let it expire;Let users register several passkeys, and name and remove them;Keep account recovery as strong as the passkey, not a weak fallback;Accept synced passkeys, and use the backup flags only if policy requires device-bound keys
done_when: Signing in with a passkey works, and a replayed response is rejected;Users can add and remove passkeys from their account

name: Bot protection
explanation: Stopping automated scripts from creating fake accounts, stuffing stolen passwords or spamming forms.
synonyms: captcha;anti-bot;recaptcha;turnstile;credential stuffing;honeypot field
triggers: stop bots;fake sign ups;spam bots;bots signing up;automated attacks;bot traffic;fake accounts
requirements: Rate-limit sign-up, login and other forms that bots target;Show a challenge, such as a CAPTCHA, only when behaviour looks suspicious;Choose an accessible challenge, with an alternative to visual puzzles;Stop credential stuffing by checking breached passwords and unusual sign-in patterns;Add a hidden honeypot field to simple forms;Watch sign-up and login numbers, and alert on sudden spikes
done_when: Scripted mass sign-ups are blocked or slowed down;People using screen readers can still complete the forms

name: Security headers
explanation: HTTP response headers, such as Content Security Policy, that tell browsers how to protect your pages.
synonyms: content security policy;csp;clickjacking;x-frame-options;http security headers
triggers: security headers;stop my site being framed;embedded in an iframe;iframe attack;harden the website;browser security;iframe;in an iframe
requirements: Set a Content Security Policy that allows only your own scripts, using nonces or hashes, not unsafe-inline;Stop other sites framing your pages with CSP frame-ancestors, or X-Frame-Options DENY;Send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff;Set a Referrer-Policy, such as strict-origin-when-cross-origin;Remove headers that reveal software versions, such as X-Powered-By;Set Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy to isolate your pages from other windows;Load third-party scripts and styles with Subresource Integrity
done_when: A header scanner such as securityheaders.com finds CSP, frame-ancestors, nosniff and Referrer-Policy set;Embedding your pages in an iframe on another site is blocked

name: Encrypting sensitive data
explanation: Protecting stored data, such as personal details or tokens, so it stays unreadable if it is stolen.
synonyms: encryption at rest;field encryption;key management;kms;secrets vault
triggers: encrypt data;encrypt sensitive;store sensitive data;protect personal data;encrypt the database;store credit card;keep data safe;id numbers;sensitive information
requirements: Store only the sensitive data you really need;Encrypt sensitive data at rest with a standard algorithm, such as AES-GCM, from a well-known library;Keep keys in a key management service or vault, separate from the data, and rotate them;Never invent your own cryptography, and never use ECB mode, MD5 or SHA-1 for security;Give the app's database user only the rights it needs, and keep the database off the public internet;Hash passwords instead of encrypting them
done_when: Stolen database files or backups reveal no readable sensitive data;No plaintext keys are in the code, the repository or the database

name: Dependency security
explanation: Keeping the libraries, packages and third-party scripts your app uses free of known vulnerabilities and tampering.
synonyms: supply chain security;dependency scanning;sbom;dependabot;npm audit
triggers: vulnerable packages;outdated dependencies;update dependencies;third party scripts;npm packages;libraries are safe;malicious package
requirements: Commit a lock file, and install exactly from it in CI, such as with npm ci;Scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities automatically, and update promptly;Check new packages before adding them: maintenance, popularity and the exact name, to avoid typosquatting;Pin CI actions to full commit hashes, and build tools to exact versions;Load third-party scripts with Subresource Integrity, or host them yourself;Produce a software bill of materials (SBOM) for each release;Remove dependencies you no longer use
done_when: The build fails or warns on dependencies with known critical vulnerabilities;Every dependency version is fixed by the lock file

name: Injection prevention
explanation: Keeping user input from being run as code or commands, in SQL, shell commands, templates, XML and more.
synonyms: command injection;nosql injection;xxe;template injection;prototype pollution;insecure deserialization
triggers: run a shell command;user input in a query;build a sql query;parse xml;eval user input;execute a command;unserialize
requirements: Use parameterized queries or an ORM for every database query, including NoSQL filters;Never pass user input to a shell, and run programs with an argument list instead;Never pass user input to eval, template compilers or other dynamic code;Turn off external entities and DTDs in XML parsers;Never deserialize untrusted data with native formats such as pickle or Java serialization;Escape user input in LDAP and XPath queries, or avoid building them from strings;Block __proto__, constructor and prototype keys when merging user JSON into objects;Run the database and services with the fewest privileges they need
done_when: Injection payloads in every input are treated as plain data;Security scanners find no injection problems

name: Fetching URLs safely (SSRF)
explanation: Letting the server fetch a URL a user supplies, such as for link previews, without exposing internal systems.
synonyms: ssrf;server side request forgery;url fetching
triggers: fetch a url;link preview;import from a url;load an image from a url;user enters a url;download from a link;url preview;pastes a link;paste a link;preview of a link
requirements: Allow only http and https, and only the hosts you expect where possible;Resolve the host, block private, loopback, link-local and metadata IPs, and connect only to the IP you checked (DNS rebinding);Check every redirect the same way, or turn redirects off;Set short timeouts and a maximum response size;Send these requests from an isolated network or proxy without access to internal services
done_when: A URL pointing at localhost, an internal address or the cloud metadata address is refused;A redirect to an internal address is refused too

name: Privacy and personal data
explanation: Handling people's personal data lawfully and carefully, as laws such as the GDPR require.
synonyms: data protection;privacy;personal data;ccpa;right to be forgotten
triggers: delete my account;export my data;personal information;privacy policy;user data;data retention;anonymize data;delete their account;delete account;all their data
requirements: Collect only the personal data you need, and explain why in a privacy notice;Let users download their data and delete their account;Delete or anonymize personal data when it is no longer needed;Limit who can access personal data, and log that access;Keep personal data out of logs, analytics and error reports;Check where third-party services store the data you send them;Ask for device permissions only when needed, and never track users with hardware identifiers
done_when: Deleting an account removes or anonymizes the user's personal data everywhere, backups on schedule;Users can download a copy of their data

name: Failed login throttling and account lockout
explanation: Slowing down or temporarily blocking sign-in attempts after repeated wrong passwords, so attackers cannot guess passwords without locking real users out of their accounts.
synonyms: account lockout;login throttling;brute force protection;failed login attempts limit;login rate limiting
triggers: too many wrong passwords;lock account after failed attempts;stop password guessing;limit login attempts;temporarily lock the account;someone keeps guessing my password
requirements: Count failed attempts per account, not only per IP address, so attacks spread over many IPs are still slowed;Cap consecutive failures per account (NIST allows at most 100) and reset the count after a successful login;Prefer growing delays or a CAPTCHA over a hard lockout so an attacker cannot lock out real users at will;Unlock automatically after a set time and offer a safe self-service path such as a reset email;Show the same message for a locked account and a wrong password so lockout does not reveal which accounts exist;Log every lockout and failed attempt burst and alert on attacks across many accounts (password spraying)
done_when: Repeated wrong passwords for one account are slowed or blocked even when sent from many IP addresses;A real user can still sign in or recover after the lockout period without contacting support;Lockouts and failure bursts appear in the security logs

name: Breached password screening
explanation: Checking a new password against lists of passwords leaked in data breaches and very common passwords, and asking the user to pick another one if it matches.
synonyms: compromised password check;password blocklist;pwned passwords;common password check;password denylist
triggers: stop people using leaked passwords;check password against breaches;block common passwords;password found in data breach;password was in a data leak;reject password123
requirements: Check every new password at sign-up, change and reset against a list of breached and commonly used passwords;Tell the user plainly why the password was rejected and ask them to choose a different one;Query an online breach service with a k-anonymity hash prefix so the full password or hash never leaves your server;Do not add composition rules such as forcing symbols or regular expiry, as NIST SP 800-63B advises against them;Allow long passphrases and paste from password managers so users can pick strong passwords;Decide how to behave when the breach service is down and keep a local list of the most common passwords

name: Account enumeration prevention
explanation: Making sign-in, sign-up and password reset respond the same way whether or not an account exists, so attackers cannot find out who has an account.

triggers: don't reveal if email is registered;login error says user not found;hide which accounts exist;same message for wrong email or password;check if someone has an account
requirements: Show one generic message such as Invalid email or password for any failed sign-in;On password reset always say If an account exists we sent an email, whether or not it exists;On sign-up send an email to an already registered address instead of saying it is taken on screen;Return the same HTTP status and similar response time for existing and unknown accounts, for example by hashing anyway;Rate limit sign-in, sign-up and reset endpoints so lookups cannot be done in bulk;Check APIs, mobile apps and error codes too, not only the web form messages

name: Magic link login
explanation: Passwordless sign-in where the user types their email and gets a link that logs them in once, for a short time, when they click it.

triggers: log in with a link by email;sign in without a password;send me a login link;email me a link to log in;no password login by email
requirements: Generate the token with a secure random generator and store only its hash on the server;Make the link single use and expire it quickly, and invalidate older links when a new one is requested;Show the same message whether or not the email has an account;Open a page that needs a click to finish signing in so email scanners that prefetch links do not use up the token;Set Referrer-Policy no-referrer on the landing page so the token does not leak to other sites;Start a new session after the link is used and rate limit link requests per email and IP

name: Account recovery after losing MFA
explanation: A safe way for users who lost their phone or security key, and their backup codes, to prove who they are and get back into their account.
synonyms: mfa reset;2fa recovery;lost authenticator recovery;mfa account recovery;second factor reset
triggers: lost my phone with authenticator;can't get 2fa code;new phone lost 2fa;reset two factor for a user;lost my security key;locked out without backup codes
requirements: Offer backup codes and let users register more than one factor so most never need recovery;Never let a password reset alone remove MFA, as that makes the second factor pointless;Require strong proof of identity such as a remaining factor or a documented ID check, not answers support can look up;Add a waiting period before the factor is removed and notify every known contact so the real owner can stop it;Make help-desk agents follow a written procedure and log who reset MFA, when and on what evidence;Ask the user to set up a new factor right after recovery and end all existing sessions

name: Step-up authentication (re-authentication)
explanation: Asking a signed-in user to enter their password or second factor again before a sensitive action, such as changing their email or sending money.

triggers: ask for password again before deleting account;confirm identity before sensitive action;enter password to continue;verify again before payment;re-enter password for settings
requirements: List which actions need fresh authentication, such as changing password, email, MFA or payout details;Check on the server how long ago the user last authenticated, not only a flag set by the client;Accept the strongest factor the user has, such as a passkey or MFA, and not only the password;Keep the elevated state short lived and tied to the current session;Also ask again after suspicious signs such as a new device or IP during the session;Return the user to the action they started after they confirm, keeping what they typed

name: Change password while signed in

triggers: change my password;update my password in settings;old password and new password;change password page;new password must differ from old
requirements: Require the current password, or recent re-authentication, before accepting a new one;Screen the new password against breached and common passwords and enforce a minimum length;Use autocomplete=current-password and new-password so password managers can fill and save them;Hash the new password with the same strong hashing as at sign-up;Send a notification to the account email that the password changed;Offer to end, or end by default, all other sessions and remember-me tokens

name: Change account email address
explanation: Letting a user switch the email they sign in with, by re-checking who they are, confirming the new address and warning the old one.

triggers: change my email address;update my email in settings;switch account to new email;i no longer use my old email;confirm the new email address
requirements: Ask for the current password or second factor before starting the change;Send a confirmation link with a short-lived single-use token to the new address and keep the old one until it is confirmed;Send a notice to the old address with a way to report and undo an unwanted change;Do not reveal on screen whether the new address already belongs to another account;Keep the old address recorded for a while so a hijacked account can be recovered;Log the change and invalidate pending password reset links

explanation: Keeping a user signed in after they close the browser, using a separate long-lived token that can be replaced and revoked.

triggers: keep users logged in after closing the browser;remember me checkbox;don't make me log in every time;stay logged in for 30 days
requirements: Make remember me opt in and leave it off by default on shared devices;Use a random token stored hashed on the server, separate from the session ID, and never store the password;Set the cookie HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite with a fixed maximum lifetime;Replace the token each time it is used and treat reuse of an old token as theft;Revoke all remembered tokens when the password changes or the user signs out everywhere;Ask for re-authentication before sensitive actions even when signed in by a remembered token

explanation: A page where users see every device and browser they are signed in on and can sign out of any one of them, or all of them at once.

name: Account security notifications
explanation: Telling users by email or push when something important happens on their account, such as a sign-in from a new device or a password or MFA change.

triggers: email me when someone logs in;alert on new device login;notify when password changes;suspicious login email;tell user their account changed
requirements: Send alerts for password, email, MFA and recovery changes and for sign-ins from new devices;Say what happened, when, and from which device and approximate location;Give a clear way to report it was not you, such as securing the account, without asking for a password in the email;Send changes of contact details to the old address as well as the new one;Do not let users turn off the critical alerts that protect against account takeover;Keep messages free of secrets and links that sign the user in

explanation: Changing what a user must do to sign in based on how risky the attempt looks, for example asking for a second factor only on a new device or from an unusual place.

name: Linking social and SSO accounts
explanation: Connecting several sign-in methods, such as a password, Google and Apple, to one user account without letting an attacker take it over.

triggers: sign in with google and password for same account;connect my apple login;add another login method;same email different login;two accounts with same email

name: Token handling in browser apps (BFF)

explanation: Letting a device with no browser or keyboard, such as a smart TV or command-line tool, sign in by showing a short code that the user enters on their phone or computer.

triggers: keep track of security issues;how fast to fix vulnerabilities;prioritise security fixes;patch known vulnerabilities;backlog of security findings
requirements: Keep an inventory of software, dependencies and systems so you know what each new vulnerability affects;Collect findings from scanners, pentests, reports and advisories in one tracker;Prioritise by severity, known exploitation and exposure, not by CVSS score alone;Set fix deadlines per severity and track overdue items;Record accepted risks with an owner, a reason and a review date;Verify fixes by rescanning or retesting before closing them;Plan how to patch quickly in an emergency
done_when: Every open finding has a severity, an owner and a due date;A report shows overdue findings;Fixed findings are verified before they are closed

name: Security incident response
explanation: Having a plan, roles and tools ready to detect, contain, investigate and recover from a security incident such as a breach or a compromised account, and to learn from it.
synonyms: security incident handling;breach response;csirt;compromise response;security incident plan
triggers: we got hacked;what to do after a breach;account was compromised;contain an attack;hacker in our systems;ransomware response
requirements: Write a plan with roles, contacts, severity levels and who can make decisions;Keep logs and alerts that let you detect incidents and reconstruct what happened;Contain first: isolate systems, revoke credentials and block the attacker's access;Preserve evidence before wiping or rebuilding systems;Remove the cause and restore from known-good backups;Check legal and contractual notification duties early;Practise the plan with tabletop exercises;Hold a lessons-learned review and track its actions
done_when: The plan names an owner and an out-of-hours contact;A tabletop exercise was run and its gaps were fixed;Credentials can be revoked across all systems quickly;Lessons-learned actions are tracked to completion

name: Personal data breach notification
explanation: Deciding whether a leak or loss of personal data must be reported, and if so telling the regulator in time (72 hours under GDPR) and telling the affected people when the risk to them is high.
synonyms: gdpr breach notification;personal data breach;article 33 notification;breach reporting;72-hour rule
triggers: we leaked customer data;do we have to report the breach;tell users their data was exposed;report to the data protection authority;email sent to the wrong customer
requirements: Notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to risk people's rights;Give reasons for any delay past 72 hours, and send information in phases if needed;Describe what happened, the data and people affected, likely consequences, measures taken and a contact;Tell affected people without undue delay when the risk to them is high, in plain language;Require processors to notify you without undue delay;Record every breach, even unreported ones, with its facts, effects and actions;Check other laws and contracts that set their own deadlines
done_when: A breach register records every incident, including unreported ones;Template notifications are ready for the regulator and for individuals;The team knows who decides whether to notify within 72 hours

name: Security event logging and alerting
explanation: Recording security-relevant events such as failed logins, access denials and permission changes in a consistent format, and raising alerts when patterns look like an attack.
synonyms: security logging;security monitoring;siem;logging vocabulary;intrusion detection alerts
triggers: alert on failed logins;detect brute force attempts;log permission changes;notice suspicious activity;monitor for attacks
requirements: Log logins, failures, logouts, access denials, input validation failures, admin actions and privilege changes;Record when, where, who and what for each event, with synchronised timestamps;Use consistent event names, such as the OWASP Logging Vocabulary;Send logs to a central store the application cannot alter or delete;Alert on patterns such as many failed logins or a new admin account;Protect logs from tampering and limit who can read them;Test that alerts reach someone who can act on them
done_when: Failed logins and permission changes appear in the central log with user, time and source;A simulated brute force attack raises an alert;Application servers cannot edit or delete stored logs

name: Keeping secrets and personal data out of logs
explanation: Keeping passwords, tokens, card numbers and other personal or secret data out of logs, and stopping user input from forging or breaking log entries.
synonyms: log redaction;log masking;log scrubbing;cwe-532;log injection prevention;pii in logs
triggers: passwords showing in logs;remove personal data from logs;mask tokens in logs;fake log entries;api keys in log files
requirements: Never log passwords, session IDs, access tokens, keys or full card numbers;Mask or hash personal data, or log an internal ID instead;Log an allow list of fields in structured logs instead of whole objects or requests;Strip query strings and headers that may carry tokens from request logs;Encode CR, LF and delimiters in user input to prevent log injection;Apply the same rules to error tracking, analytics and debug logs;Set retention limits and access controls for logs
done_when: Logging in with a test password leaves no trace of it in any log;A username containing a newline cannot create a fake log line;A scan of the logs finds no tokens or card numbers

name: Web application firewall (WAF)
explanation: A filter in front of your app that inspects each web request and blocks ones that look like common attacks, such as SQL injection or cross-site scripting. It has to be tuned so it does not block real users.
synonyms: waf;owasp core rule set;layer 7 firewall;application firewall rules
triggers: block malicious requests;filter attack traffic;firewall in front of the app;waf blocking real users;false positives from firewall;block known attack patterns
requirements: Start in detection-only or log mode and review hits on real traffic before blocking;Start with the least strict rule level, such as CRS paranoia level 1, and raise it only after tuning false positives;Write rule exclusions as narrow as possible, for one parameter on one path, never disable a rule globally;Pass the real client IP from the proxy or CDN so logs and blocks target the right address;Decide what happens to request bodies larger than the inspection limit instead of letting them through silently;Keep fixing the app itself: a WAF reduces risk but does not replace secure code;Update the rule set regularly and re-test after each update
done_when: Known attack payloads such as a SQL injection string are blocked or logged;Normal user journeys, including forms with free text and file uploads, pass without being blocked;Each block is logged with the rule id, client IP and request path;There is a documented way to add an exclusion when a real user is blocked

name: Denial-of-service protection
explanation: Keeping an application available when someone floods it with traffic or sends requests designed to use up memory, CPU or connections. It combines limits and timeouts in the app with filtering in front of it.
synonyms: dos protection;ddos mitigation;resource exhaustion;traffic flood protection;layer 7 ddos
triggers: site goes down under heavy traffic;flooded with requests;stop traffic floods;attack takes the site offline;survive a ddos attack;someone flooding our site
requirements: Put a CDN or upstream DDoS filtering service in front of public endpoints;Set timeouts for reading request headers and bodies, and for calls to databases and other services;Limit request body size, upload size, page size and query complexity;Rate-limit expensive or unauthenticated operations such as search, login and report generation;Cap concurrent connections and requests per client;Avoid costly work before authentication, such as heavy parsing or sending email;Set autoscaling limits and spending alerts so a flood cannot cause an unbounded bill;Hide origin server IPs so attackers cannot bypass the upstream filter
done_when: A load test with many slow or oversized requests does not make the app unavailable to normal users;Requests over the size or rate limits are rejected quickly with a clear error;The origin server refuses traffic that does not come through the CDN or filter;Alerts fire when traffic or error rates spike

name: Email sender authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)
explanation: DNS records that prove email really comes from your domain: SPF lists the servers allowed to send, DKIM signs each message, and DMARC tells receivers what to do with mail that fails. Together they stop others spoofing your domain and help your mail reach inboxes.
synonyms: spf;dkim;dmarc;email authentication;email spoofing protection
triggers: emails going to spam;stop people faking our email address;spoofed emails from our domain;set up dns for sending email;email not delivered to inbox;phishing using our domain
requirements: Publish one SPF record listing every service that sends mail for the domain, and keep it within the 10 DNS lookup limit;Sign mail with DKIM for every sending service, using keys of at least 1024 bits and preferably 2048;Make sure the visible From domain aligns with the SPF or DKIM domain, or DMARC will fail;Start DMARC with p=none and a rua address to collect reports, then move to quarantine and reject;Read the DMARC reports to find legitimate senders that fail before tightening the policy;Protect domains that send no mail with SPF -all and a DMARC reject policy;Rotate DKIM keys and remove records for services you no longer use
done_when: Test messages from each sending service pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC in the received headers;The domain has a DMARC policy of quarantine or reject;DMARC aggregate reports arrive and show no unexplained failing sources;Parked domains reject spoofed mail

name: Subdomain takeover prevention
explanation: Stopping attackers from taking over one of your subdomains when its DNS record still points to a cloud service, bucket or hosting account you have deleted. Whoever claims that resource can then serve content on your domain.
synonyms: subdomain takeover;dangling dns records;dangling cname;stale dns entries
triggers: old subdomain still points to deleted app;cname to deleted service;someone hijacked our subdomain;clean up old dns records;deleted bucket still in dns
requirements: Keep an inventory of every DNS record with an owner and the resource it points to;Remove or update the DNS record before deleting the cloud resource it points to;Check CNAME, A, AAAA and NS records for targets that no longer exist or are unclaimed;Watch for delegated NS records pointing to zones that no longer exist;Use the cloud provider's domain verification feature where it is offered;Scan DNS regularly for dangling records and alert on them;Avoid wildcard DNS records that point to shared hosting
done_when: Every DNS record maps to a resource your organization still owns;A scheduled scan for dangling records runs and reports none;The decommissioning checklist includes removing DNS records first

name: Masking sensitive data in the UI
explanation: Showing only part of a sensitive value, such as the last four digits of a card or ID number, so people who do not need the full value never see it. Some roles may reveal the full value, and that is logged.
synonyms: data masking;partial masking;pan masking;redacted display;dynamic data masking
triggers: show only last 4 digits;hide card number on screen;hide part of the id number;mask account numbers for staff;reveal full number button
requirements: Mask on the server so the full value never reaches a client that should not see it, not with CSS or front-end code;Show card numbers with no more than the BIN (first 6 or 8) and last 4 digits, as PCI DSS allows;Decide per role who may see the full value, and default to masked;Log every reveal of a full value with who, when and why;Mask the same value consistently in emails, exports, receipts, logs and support tools;Keep masked values from being copied back as if they were real when a form is saved
done_when: Users without permission never receive the full value in API responses;Support staff see only the masked form in admin screens and exports;Revealing a full value creates an audit log entry;Saving a form that shows a masked value does not overwrite the stored value

name: Crypto-shredding (cryptographic erase)
explanation: Making data unreadable by destroying the encryption key that protects it, instead of finding and deleting every copy. It is useful for data in backups, logs or storage you cannot easily erase.
synonyms: cryptographic erase;crypto shredding;key destruction;cryptographic deletion
triggers: delete data from backups;erase data we cannot delete;delete user data in old backups;destroy the encryption key;make deleted data unreadable
requirements: Encrypt the data from the start with keys scoped to what you will need to erase, such as one key per customer or tenant;Store keys in a key management service, never next to the data or inside the backups;Delete every copy of the key, including key backups, caches and escrow, and log the destruction;Check that no unencrypted copies exist in logs, search indexes, caches or analytics;Allow for the key service deletion waiting period, often 7 to 30 days, when promising an erasure date;Record which key protects which data so you can find the key to destroy
done_when: After the key is destroyed, restored backups cannot decrypt that customer's data;No plaintext copy of the data remains in other systems;Key destruction is recorded with date and reason

name: Consent management and records
explanation: Asking people for clear, opt-in permission for each separate use of their data, keeping a record of what they agreed to and when, and letting them withdraw it as easily as they gave it.
synonyms: consent records;consent management platform;cmp;opt-in consent;granular consent;consent withdrawal
triggers: record when users agreed;let users withdraw permission;separate opt-ins for marketing;proof of consent;manage what users agreed to;unticked opt-in box
requirements: Ask for consent separately for each purpose, not bundled with terms and conditions;Use unticked boxes or equivalent active opt-in, never pre-ticked or assumed consent;Name your organization and any third parties that rely on the consent;Record who consented, when, how, and the exact wording they saw;Make withdrawing as easy as giving consent and act on it in every system;Do not make a service conditional on consent that it does not need;Review and refresh consent when the purpose or wording changes
done_when: Each purpose has its own opt-in that starts unchecked;The record for a user shows the wording, time and method of each consent;Withdrawing consent stops the processing in all connected systems;Users can see and change their consents from their account

name: Do Not Sell or Share opt-out (GPC)
explanation: Letting people opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal data, for example for targeted advertising, through a link and by honouring the Global Privacy Control signal that browsers can send automatically.
synonyms: global privacy control;gpc;do not sell my personal information;opt-out preference signal;sec-gpc header
triggers: do not sell my info link;opt out of selling data;honour browser privacy signal;stop sharing data with advertisers;opt out of targeted ads
requirements: Treat the Sec-GPC: 1 request header or navigator.globalPrivacyControl as a valid opt-out of sale and sharing;Apply the opt-out to the browser and, when the user is signed in, to their account;Stop passing the person's data to advertising and data-sharing third parties once they opt out;Offer a clear Do Not Sell or Share link that works without requiring an account;Do not ask for more information than needed to process the opt-out;Show the user that their opt-out request was honoured;Wait at least 12 months before asking an opted-out user to opt back in to sale or sharing
done_when: A browser sending Sec-GPC: 1 loads no advertising or data-selling tags;A signed-in user's opt-out follows them to other devices;The opt-out link works for visitors without an account

name: Data subject access and portability requests
explanation: Letting people ask for a copy of all the personal data you hold about them, checking who they are, and sending it in a readable and reusable format within the legal time limit.
synonyms: subject access request;dsar;sar;right of access;data portability;right to data portability
triggers: give users a copy of their data;request all my personal data;download everything you have on me;handle data access requests;legal request for user data
requirements: Respond within one month, extendable by two more months only for complex or numerous requests;Verify identity in proportion to the risk, without asking for more data than needed;Search every system, including logs, backups in use, support tools and third-party processors;Include the purposes, recipients, retention period and source of the data, not just the raw data;Give data the person provided in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format such as JSON or CSV;Remove other people's personal data from the copy before sending it;Deliver the copy securely and track each request with its deadline
done_when: A test request returns data from every system that holds the person's data;Requests are logged with received date and due date;The export opens in common tools and contains no other people's data

name: Data anonymisation
explanation: Changing personal data so that nobody can be identified from it, even by combining it with other data, so it can be used for analytics, research or sharing. Done properly, the result is no longer personal data.
synonyms: anonymization;de-identification;k-anonymity;data aggregation;statistical disclosure control
triggers: anonymise data for analytics;remove names before sharing data;share data without identifying people;make the dataset non identifiable;re-identification risk
requirements: Remove direct identifiers and also generalise or suppress indirect ones such as postcode, birth date and rare values;Aggregate results and suppress small counts that could single out a person;Test re-identification with a motivated intruder test against data that is publicly available;Consider who will receive the data and what else they could combine it with;Do not call hashed or tokenised data anonymous: that is pseudonymisation;Document the method and reassess the risk when the data or its use changes
done_when: A motivated intruder test fails to identify individuals in the output;No row or small group can be singled out by its combination of attributes;The method and risk assessment are documented

name: Pseudonymisation
explanation: Replacing names, emails and other direct identifiers with tokens or keyed hashes, so the data cannot be linked to a person without extra information that is kept separately and protected.
synonyms: pseudonymization;tokenization of personal data;keyed hashing;hmac pseudonyms;data tokenisation
triggers: replace user ids with tokens;hide identities in analytics data;hash emails before sharing;separate identity from the data
requirements: Use a keyed hash such as HMAC with a secret key, or random tokens, not a plain hash of the identifier;Store the key or token mapping separately, with stricter access than the pseudonymised data;Use different keys for different recipients or purposes so their datasets cannot be linked;Check that remaining fields, such as free text or rare values, do not identify people anyway;Treat pseudonymised data as personal data: it still needs a legal basis and protection;Log and restrict re-identification to approved cases
done_when: The pseudonymised dataset contains no names, emails or other direct identifiers;People with access to the dataset have no access to the key or mapping;Two recipients' datasets use different pseudonyms for the same person

name: Data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
explanation: A structured review done before launching something that uses personal data in a risky way, such as large-scale tracking or sensitive data, to find the privacy risks and decide how to reduce them.
synonyms: dpia;privacy impact assessment;pia;privacy risk assessment
triggers: privacy review before launch;assess privacy risks of a feature;is this processing high risk;privacy assessment for new system
requirements: Run it before processing starts, for high-risk uses such as profiling, large-scale sensitive data or systematic monitoring;Describe the processing: what data, whose, why, where it flows and how long it is kept;Assess whether the processing is necessary and proportionate to the purpose;Identify risks to people, not just to the organization, and rate their likelihood and severity;Record the measures that reduce each risk and who approved the remaining risk;Get advice from the data protection officer where there is one;Consult the supervisory authority before starting if high risk remains;Review the assessment when the processing changes
done_when: The DPIA is completed and signed off before launch;Each identified risk has a mitigation or an accepted owner;The DPIA is linked to the feature and has a review date

name: Records of processing activities (ROPA)
explanation: A register, kept up to date, listing each way your organization uses personal data: what data, whose, for what purpose, who receives it, where it goes and how long it is kept.
synonyms: ropa;record of processing activities;article 30 records;data processing register
triggers: list what personal data we process;register of data processing;document how we use personal data;record of where data is sent
requirements: Record the purposes, categories of people and data, recipients, and retention periods for each processing activity;Record transfers to other countries and the safeguards used;Include a general description of the security measures;Name the controller, any joint controllers and the data protection officer;Keep a separate record for processing you do on behalf of other organizations;Update the register as part of launching or changing a feature that uses personal data
done_when: Every system that holds personal data appears in the register;Each entry has a purpose, retention period and recipients;The register can be produced on request from a regulator

name: Data classification and PII inventory
explanation: Labelling data by how sensitive it is and finding where personal data is stored, so each kind gets the right level of protection.
synonyms: data classification;pii inventory;data discovery;sensitivity labels;data mapping
triggers: find where personal data is stored;label data by sensitivity;which tables contain pii;sensitive data scanning;map personal information
requirements: Define a small set of sensitivity levels with clear examples and handling rules for each;Rate the impact if each kind of personal data leaked, considering how identifying and sensitive it is;Scan databases, files, logs, backups and analytics for personal data, not just the main tables;Give each dataset an owner responsible for its classification;Carry labels with the data when it is copied, exported or sent to other systems;Minimise what you collect and keep, since data you do not hold cannot leak;Review classifications when schemas or features change
done_when: Every data store has a classification and an owner;Scans find no personal data in places it is not expected, such as logs;Each sensitivity level maps to required controls that are applied

name: Data residency and international transfers
explanation: Keeping personal data stored and processed in the regions the law or your customers require, and putting legal safeguards in place before data is sent to or accessed from another country.
synonyms: data residency;data localisation;cross-border data transfers;standard contractual clauses;data sovereignty
triggers: keep data in the eu;store data in a specific country;send personal data abroad;data must stay in region;transfer data outside europe
requirements: List every place data goes, including backups, logs, analytics, support tools and sub-processors;Pin storage and processing to the required region, including replicas and disaster recovery copies;Treat remote access from another country, such as support staff, as a transfer;Transfer only to adequate countries or with safeguards such as standard contractual clauses;Assess the risks of the destination country's laws before relying on those safeguards;Keep transfers and safeguards recorded and review them when vendors change
done_when: Data for regional customers is stored only in the agreed region, including backups;Each transfer outside the region has a documented safeguard;A list of sub-processors and their locations is kept up to date
